name: Registering and Running a Small Business in Africa
objectives: Given the size, owners and risks of your business, choose a business form, such as a sole proprietor business name or a limited company, and write why it fits, naming one benefit and one duty of the form you chose
Given the country where you trade, identify the official business registry and open its official website or office, without using an unofficial agent or a look-alike website
Before you start a registration, prepare a registration checklist with three name choices, owner details, business activity, address and documents, so the application can be filled in at one sitting
For your business and town, list the tax number, local trade permit and any sector permit that apply, and where to get each, with the official office checked for each one
Over one week of trading, record every sale and every cost in a simple cash book, kept apart from household money, with the week's money in and money out adding up
Once your business is registered, draw up a yearly calendar of renewals, returns and permit dates, with each date checked on the official site and a reminder set before it

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Why register, and which business form fits you
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose a business form that fits your business and write down why.
This lesson builds toward: Given the size, owners and risks of your business, you will choose a business form, such as a sole proprietor business name or a limited company, and write why it fits, naming one benefit and one duty of the form you chose.
Registering tells the government that your business exists and gives it an official name. Benefits can include a business bank account, contracts with companies and government, selling on some marketplaces, trust from customers, and applying for loans and support programmes. Duties can include keeping records, renewing, filing returns and paying tax.
The common forms: a sole proprietorship (one owner, often registered as a business name); a partnership (two or more owners sharing profit and debt); and a limited company (a separate legal person, so the owners' homes and savings are better protected from business debts, but with more paperwork). Names differ by country: Nigeria and Ghana register business names and companies; in Kenya the Business Registration Service handles business names and companies.
In the 17 OHADA countries, including Senegal, Côte d'Ivoire, Cameroon, Mali, Burkina Faso and DR Congo, business law is shared. A small trader can register as an individual business (entreprise individuelle) or create a company such as a SARL. In Morocco, many small sellers use the auto-entrepreneur status.
Most market traders and artisans start as a sole proprietor or business name. A company may fit when you have partners, bigger contracts or bigger risks. For a big decision, ask the registry or a qualified accountant or lawyer.
Step by step:
- Write who owns the business: you alone, or with others.
- Write the biggest risk: debts, injuries, big contracts.
- Compare a business name (sole proprietor), a partnership and a company.
- Choose one and write one benefit and one duty.
Words to know:
- Sole proprietor: a business owned and run by one person, who is personally responsible for its debts.
- Limited company: a business that is its own legal person, so the owners' personal property is better protected from its debts.
- OHADA: an organisation of 17 African countries that share the same business laws, mostly in West and Central Africa.
Official sources:
- OHADA: Organisation for the Harmonisation of Business Law in Africa (17 member countries)
- Morocco: auto-entrepreneur status portal
Try it now: Write your business's owners and its biggest risk. Then choose a business form and write one benefit and one duty of that form.
You can now compare the common business forms and choose the one that fits your business.

check.q: Fatima sells fabric alone in a market in Kano. Which form do most traders like her start with?
options: A business name as a sole proprietor
check.why: One owner with a small business usually starts with a business name.

check.q: What is one main reason to choose a limited company?
options: It better protects the owners' personal property from business debts
It cannot open a bank account
check.why: A company is a separate legal person, which limits the owners' personal risk.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Finding the official registry, and avoiding fake agents
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find your country's official business registry and open its official website.
This lesson builds toward: Given the country where you trade, you will identify the official business registry and open its official website or office, without using an unofficial agent or a look-alike website.
Each country has an official office that registers businesses. Kenya: the Business Registration Service (BRS), online through eCitizen. Nigeria: the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC). Ghana: the Office of the Registrar of Companies (ORC). Senegal: APIX, the business creation one-stop shop. Côte d'Ivoire: CEPICI. In Morocco, the auto-entrepreneur status has its own national portal.
Use only the official website or office. Official government sites often end in the country's government ending, such as .go.ke, .gov.ng or .gov.gh. Look-alike websites and people offering "fast" or "free" registration exist; the Kenyan BRS site itself warns about fake "free" registration offers.
You may pay an accredited agent or lawyer to help, but check that they are real, ask for an official receipt, and make sure the business is registered in your name. Never give anyone your eCitizen, CAC or other account password, or a one-time code sent to your phone.
If a website does not open, try again later or visit the registry's office or a government service centre. Do not pay a stranger instead.
Step by step:
- Write your country's registry from the list in this lesson.
- Type its address yourself; do not click links from unknown messages.
- Check the address ending, such as .go.ke, .gov.ng or .gov.gh.
- If you use an agent, check they are real and get an official receipt.
- Never share your password or one-time code.
Words to know:
- Registry: the government office that records businesses and companies.
- Look-alike website: a fake site made to look like an official one, often to take your money.
- One-time code: a short code sent to your phone to confirm it is you; never share it.
Official sources:
- Business Registration Service, Kenya: register your business online through eCitizen
- Corporate Affairs Commission, Nigeria: company, business name and incorporated trustees registration (portal icrp.cac.gov.ng)
- Office of the Registrar of Companies, Ghana: business names, companies, renewals (including by *222#) and annual returns
- APIX, Senegal: investment promotion agency and business creation one-stop shop
- CEPICI, Côte d'Ivoire: investment promotion centre and business creation one-stop shop
- Morocco: auto-entrepreneur status portal
Try it now: Find your country's business registry. Type its website address yourself, check the ending, and write down the address and one service it lists.
You can now find your country's official business registry and tell a real site from a fake one.

check.q: Where do you register a business name in Nigeria?
check.why: The CAC registers business names, companies and incorporated trustees in Nigeria.

check.q: A message offers "free 1-hour business registration" through a link. What do you do?
options: Ignore the link and type the official registry address yourself
check.why: Fake offers use links; the official site you type yourself is safe.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Preparing your registration checklist
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Prepare a registration checklist so you can apply in one sitting.
This lesson builds toward: Before you start a registration, you will prepare a registration checklist with three name choices, owner details, business activity, address and documents, so the application can be filled in at one sitting.
Online forms can time out, and data costs money. Prepare everything first, then apply in one sitting.
Most registries ask for similar things: three possible business names (in case your first choice is taken; Kenya's BRS asks for three choices), the owners' full names and national ID or passport details, phone and email, the business address or location, a short description of the business activity, and sometimes a passport photo or a signature. A company also needs directors, shareholders and its rules. The exact list is on the registry's site.
Choose names that are clear and not already used by someone else, and that do not copy a famous brand. Example: Kofi in Takoradi lists "Kofi Fresh Fish Supplies", "Takoradi Fresh Catch" and "Sea Gold Fish Supplies".
Write down the fee shown on the official site at the time you apply, and how to pay. Keep every receipt and the registration certificate, in paper and as a photo in a safe place.
Step by step:
- Write three name choices.
- List owners' names, ID details, phone and email.
- Write the address or location and the business activity.
- Read the registry's own list for extra documents.
- Write the current fee and payment method from the official site.
- Apply in one sitting and keep every receipt and the certificate.
Words to know:
- Name search / reservation: checking that a business name is free and holding it for you while you register.
- Certificate of registration: the official paper that shows your business is registered.
- Director: a person who runs a company and has legal duties to it.
Official sources:
- Business Registration Service, Kenya: register your business online through eCitizen
- Office of the Registrar of Companies, Ghana: business names, companies, renewals (including by *222#) and annual returns
Try it now: Write your registration checklist: three name choices, owner details (without writing your ID number in any shared place), address, business activity, documents, and the registry's website.
You can now prepare a registration checklist so you can apply in one sitting.

check.q: Why prepare three business name choices?
options: In case your first choice is already taken
check.why: If your first name is taken, the next choice saves a second application.

check.q: Where do you find the exact documents your registry needs?
options: The registry's official website or office
An advert from an unknown agent
check.why: Requirements change, and only the registry is sure.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Tax number and local permits
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: List the tax number and permits your business needs and where to get each.
This lesson builds toward: For your business and town, you will list the tax number, local trade permit and any sector permit that apply, and where to get each, with the official office checked for each one.
Registering the name is often only the first step. Most businesses also need a tax identification number, a local trading permit, and, for some kinds of work, a sector permit.
Tax number: in Kenya, the KRA PIN from the Kenya Revenue Authority, which you get on iTax; it is needed for business registration and many other dealings. In Nigeria, the federal tax authority is the Nigeria Revenue Service (NRS), and each state has its own internal revenue service. In Ghana, the Ghana Revenue Authority uses your TIN or Ghana Card PIN, and lists a Modified Taxation Scheme for small businesses. Ask the tax office which small-business tax applies to you.
Local permit: many towns and counties need a trading or business permit, renewed regularly. In Kenya this is from your county government; in Nigeria from the state or local government; in Ghana from the district or municipal assembly. Sector permits: food sellers, salons, clinics, transport and others may need a health certificate or a licence from a sector body.
Ask at the local government office or a business support centre such as SMEDAN in Nigeria. Write each requirement, the office and the date you checked. Your national ID or tax number is private: do not post it or send it to strangers.
Step by step:
- Find your tax authority and ask how a small business gets a tax number.
- Ask your county, state, local government or assembly about a trading permit.
- Ask whether your kind of work needs a health certificate or sector licence.
- Write each one, the office, and the date you checked.
Words to know:
- Tax identification number (TIN): the number the tax office gives you to file and pay tax; in Kenya it is the KRA PIN.
- Trading permit: permission from your local government to run a business in that area.
- Sector permit: a licence for certain kinds of work, such as food, health or transport.
Official sources:
- Kenya Revenue Authority: about the KRA PIN (get it on iTax)
- Nigeria Revenue Service (NRS): the federal tax authority of Nigeria
- Ghana Revenue Authority: registering with a TIN or Ghana Card PIN; Modified Taxation Scheme for small businesses
- SMEDAN, Nigeria: support for nano, micro, small and medium enterprises (free registration, SME Digital Academy)
Try it now: Make a three-row table: tax number, local permit, sector permit. For each, write the office, its website or address, and whether it applies to you. Check at least one with the office this week.
You can now list the tax number and permits your business needs and the office for each.

check.q: In Kenya, how do you get a KRA PIN?
options: On iTax, from the Kenya Revenue Authority
check.why: The KRA issues the PIN through its iTax system.

check.q: Grace opens a food stall in Accra. Besides registration, what should she ask about?
options: A trading permit and any food or health certificate
check.why: Local permits and food safety requirements often apply to food sellers.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: A simple cash book: keeping business money apart
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Record every sale and every cost in a simple cash book for one week.
This lesson builds toward: Over one week of trading, you will record every sale and every cost in a simple cash book, kept apart from household money, with the week's money in and money out adding up.
Records show whether you are really making money. They also help with tax, loans and renewals. Start simple: a notebook or a phone notes page.
A cash book has four columns: date, what happened, money in, money out. Write every sale and every cost the same day, including mobile money. At the end of the day or week, add money in, add money out, and take one from the other. Example from Douala: on Monday, Paul sells 12 phone covers for 24,000 XAF and buys stock for 15,000 XAF; money in minus money out is 9,000 XAF (example figures).
Keep business money apart from household money. If you take money for food or school fees, write it as "owner took" so you can see it. A separate mobile money line or account for the business makes this easier. Keep receipts in an envelope or take photos of them.
Step by step:
- Draw four columns: date, what happened, money in, money out.
- Write every sale and cost the same day.
- Write money you take for the home as "owner took".
- At the end of the week, add each column and find the difference.
- Keep receipts in an envelope or as photos.
Words to know:
- Cash book: a simple record of money coming into and going out of the business.
- Owner took (drawings): money the owner takes out of the business for personal use.
Try it now: Start a cash book today. Write every sale and every cost for one week, including money you take for the home. On the last day, add each column and write the difference.
You can now keep a simple cash book and keep business money apart from household money.

check.q: What are the four columns of a simple cash book?
options: Date, what happened, money in, money out
check.why: These four columns show every movement of money.

check.q: You take 2,000 NGN from the business for food at home. What do you write?
check.why: Writing what the owner takes keeps the records true.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Staying registered: renewals, returns and a yearly calendar
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Draw up a yearly calendar of renewals, returns and permit dates.
This lesson builds toward: Once your business is registered, you will draw up a yearly calendar of renewals, returns and permit dates, with each date checked on the official site and a reminder set before it.
Registering once is not the end. Many businesses must renew, file annual returns or tax returns, and renew local permits. Missing a date can mean penalties or losing the registration.
Examples: Ghana's ORC says annual returns are required for all incorporated companies, and business names can be renewed online, including by dialling *222#. Nigeria's CAC oversees annual returns. Kenya's KRA expects returns from people with tax obligations. Local permits often run for a year. The exact dates and fees differ, so check each one on the official site or at the office.
Make a yearly calendar: write each duty, the office, the month it is due and the date you checked. Set a reminder on your phone one month before. Keep your cash book up to date, because returns use those numbers.
If you are unsure what applies to you, ask the registry, the tax office, a business support centre or a qualified accountant. If someone calls saying your registration will be cancelled today unless you pay them now, check with the registry yourself first.
Step by step:
- List every duty: renewal, annual return, tax return, permit renewal.
- Check each date and office on the official site.
- Write them in a 12-month calendar.
- Set a phone reminder one month before each date.
- Check rushed payment demands with the registry yourself.
Words to know:
- Annual return: a yearly report to the registry that your business still exists and its details are correct.
- Renewal: paying or filing again so a registration or permit stays valid.
- Penalty: a fine for being late or breaking a rule.
Official sources:
- Office of the Registrar of Companies, Ghana: business names, companies, renewals (including by *222#) and annual returns
- Corporate Affairs Commission, Nigeria: company, business name and incorporated trustees registration (portal icrp.cac.gov.ng)
- Kenya Revenue Authority: about the KRA PIN (get it on iTax)
Try it now: Final task: put together your registration checklist with your business form, registry, name choices, documents, tax number and permits, cash book plan and a 12-month calendar of renewals and returns with reminders set.
You can now plan your yearly renewals and returns so your business stays registered and in good standing.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Business form No form chosen, or no reason given. A form chosen with one benefit and one duty, fitting the owners and risks. Compares two forms and says when the business might change form. Official registry No registry named, or an unofficial site or agent. The correct official registry and its official website or office address. Also notes how to spot a fake site or agent. Registration checklist Missing name choices, owner details or activity. Three names, owner details, address, activity, documents and the fee from the official site. Also names the documents a company would need, or where to keep the certificate safely. Tax number and permits No tax number or permit listed, or no office named. Tax number, local permit and any sector permit, each with its office and date checked. At least one was confirmed with the office in person or by phone. Cash book No cash book, or business and home money mixed. One week of records with four columns, "owner took" entries and correct weekly totals. A separate business money line or account and receipts kept. Yearly calendar No calendar, or dates guessed. A 12-month calendar of renewals, returns and permits with offices, dates checked and reminders set. Notes who to ask (registry, tax office or accountant) for each duty. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: When should you set a reminder for a renewal?
options: About one month before it is due
check.why: A reminder a month before gives you time to prepare and pay.

check.q: A caller says your business will be cancelled today unless you pay him now. What do you do?
options: Check with the registry yourself before paying anyone
check.why: Rushed payment demands are a scam sign; the registry itself can tell you your status.
